questions.question: As per Article 118 of the Constitution of India, who presides over the joint sitting of the two houses?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Speaker**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• As per Article 118 of the Indian Constitution, the Speaker of the Lok Sabha presides over the joint sitting of both the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha.
 
• The joint sitting is convened by the President of India in cases where there is a deadlock over a bill between the two houses.
 
• The provision for a joint sitting applies only to ordinary bills and not to money bills or constitutional amendment bills.
 
• If the Speaker is unavailable, the Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha presides over the joint sitting.
 
• This mechanism ensures resolution of legislative disagreements between the two houses of Parliament.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Article 118:** It provides for the rules and procedures of Parliament, including provisions for joint sittings.
 
• **Deadlock Resolution:** Joint sittings are convened to resolve legislative disagreements between the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha, ensuring smooth passage of bills.
 
• **Exclusions:** Joint sittings cannot be called for money bills or constitutional amendment bills, as their procedures are explicitly defined in the Constitution.
 
• **Role of President:** The President of India summons the joint sitting, but the Speaker presides over it.
 
• **Historical Example:** The first-ever joint sitting of Parliament was held in 1961 to pass the Dowry Prohibition Act after disagreements between the two houses.

questions.question: In 1953,who among the following dancers was called to perform for the coronation festivities of Queen Elizabeth (II)?
questions.solution:

• **Kumari Kamala**, a renowned Bharatanatyam dancer, was invited to perform during the coronation festivities of **Queen Elizabeth II in 1953**.
 
• She was celebrated for her exceptional contributions to Indian classical dance, particularly in Bharatanatyam, which showcased India's rich cultural heritage on the global stage.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Bharatanatyam**

 
 
• Bharatanatyam is one of the oldest classical dance forms of India, originating from Tamil Nadu.
 
• It combines **expressive gestures (mudras)**, rhythmic movements, and storytelling to depict themes from Hindu mythology.
 
• The dance form is deeply rooted in the Natya Shastra, an ancient Sanskrit text on performing arts.
 
• Bharatanatyam is traditionally performed by solo dancers and is known for its intricate footwork and precise expressions.
 
 
 
• **Coronation of Queen Elizabeth II**
 
 
• Queen Elizabeth II was crowned on **June 2, 1953**, at Westminster Abbey in London.
 
• The coronation was a grand event attended by dignitaries and representatives from across the world.
 
• The festivities included cultural performances from various countries, reflecting the global reach of the British Empire at the time.
 
 
 
• **Indian Classical Dance**

• Each dance form is unique in its style, costumes, music, and storytelling techniques.
 
• These dances are often deeply spiritual and are performed to express devotion and tell mythological tales.

questions.question: The chemical name of baking soda is:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**sodium hydrogen carbonate (NaHCO3)**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The chemical name of baking soda is **sodium hydrogen carbonate (NaHCO3)**, also commonly known as bicarbonate of soda.
 
• Baking soda is a white crystalline solid but often appears as a fine powder.
 
• It is widely used as a leavening agent in cooking, especially in baking, where it reacts with acidic components to release carbon dioxide gas, causing the dough to rise.
 
• It is mildly alkaline and can neutralize acids, which is why it is used for relieving indigestion and as a cleaning agent.
 
• Baking soda decomposes at high temperatures to form sodium carbonate (Na2CO3), water (H2O), and carbon dioxide (CO2).

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Leavening Agent:**

 
 
• Baking soda acts as a leavening agent in baked goods by reacting with acids like vinegar, yogurt, or lemon juice to release carbon dioxide gas.
 
 
 
• **Neutralization Reaction:**
 
 
• It neutralizes acidic substances, making it useful in antacids for relieving heartburn and indigestion.
 
 
 
• **Cleaning Agent:**
 
 
• Baking soda is commonly used as a household cleaning agent due to its ability to dissolve dirt and grease.
 
• It is also used to deodorize refrigerators and carpets.
 
 
 
• **Decomposition of Baking Soda:**
 
 
• When heated, sodium hydrogen carbonate decomposes into sodium carbonate, water, and carbon dioxide, which is why it is used in fire extinguishers.
 
 
 
• **Difference from Baking Powder:**
 
 
• Baking powder contains sodium hydrogen carbonate and an acidic component, allowing it to work without additional acids, unlike baking soda.

questions.question: Which among the following is NOT a basic attribute of Dhamma mentioned in the Ashokan edicts?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Celibacy**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Ashoka’s concept of Dhamma, as mentioned in his edicts, emphasizes moral and ethical behavior essential for societal harmony.
 
• The main attributes of Dhamma include truthfulness, compassion, charity, tolerance, and respect for others.
 
• Celibacy is not mentioned as a basic attribute of Dhamma in the Ashokan edicts.
 
• Ashoka’s Dhamma was primarily aimed at ensuring peace, coexistence, and social welfare rather than imposing ascetic practices like celibacy.
 
• The concept was influenced by Buddhist principles but was designed to cater to a broader audience, including non-Buddhists.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Ashoka’s Dhamma:**

 
 
• Dhamma is not a religion but a set of ethical guidelines aimed at promoting harmony and welfare.
 
• Ashoka propagated Dhamma through inscriptions on pillars, rocks, and edicts across his empire.
 
• It included principles like non-violence (Ahimsa), respect for elders, kindness to animals, and religious tolerance.
 
• The concept sought to address social issues such as caste discrimination and promote unity.
 
 
 
• **Ashokan Edicts:**
 
 
• The edicts are inscriptions carved on rocks and pillars across India and neighboring regions.
 
• They serve as a record of Ashoka’s policies and ideals, especially his adoption of Dhamma after the Kalinga War.
 
• The inscriptions were written in Prakrit, Greek, and Aramaic using scripts like Brahmi and Kharosthi.
 
• These edicts reflect Ashoka’s efforts to spread Dhamma and establish ethical governance.
 
 
 
• **Kalinga War:**
 
 
• The Kalinga War (circa 261 BCE) was a turning point in Ashoka’s life and reign.
 
• The immense suffering caused by the war led Ashoka to embrace Buddhism and adopt a policy of non-violence.
 
• Post-war, Ashoka focused on moral governance and welfare activities for his subjects.
 
 
 
• **Buddhist Influence on Dhamma:**
 
 
• Ashoka was deeply influenced by Buddhist teachings, particularly the emphasis on compassion and non-violence.
 
• While Dhamma incorporated Buddhist principles, it was designed to be inclusive for followers of other religions.
 
• Buddhist monks played a key role in spreading Dhamma across Ashoka’s empire and beyond to regions like Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia.

questions.question: What is the ornate mountain-like entrance gateway before entering the premises of temples located in South India called?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Gopuram**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The term **Gopuram** refers to the monumental tower at the entrance of temple premises, commonly found in South Indian temple architecture.
 
• Gopurams are intricately decorated with carvings of deities, mythological stories, and other symbolic motifs, showcasing the region's rich cultural and religious traditions.
 
• These gateways are primarily constructed in the **Dravidian architectural style**, which is predominant in Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, and Kerala.
 
• In many temples, the gopurams are the tallest structures, symbolizing the connection between the earthly realm and the divine.
 
• The **Meenakshi Temple in Madurai** and the **Brihadeeswarar Temple in Thanjavur** are famous for their grand and elaborately designed gopurams.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Dravidian Architecture:**

 
 
• A style of temple architecture developed in South India, characterized by pyramid-shaped towers (vimanas) and large gateways (gopurams).
 
• Features extensive use of stone and intricate carvings of gods, celestial beings, and mythological narratives.
 
 
 
• **Key Parts of a South Indian Temple:**
 
 
• **Garbhagriha:** The innermost sanctum where the main deity resides.
 
• **Mandapa:** The pillared hall for devotees to gather.
 
• **Gopuram:** The monumental tower at the entrance.
 
• **Prakaram:** Enclosure walls surrounding the temple.
 
 
 
• **Symbolism of the Gopuram:**
 
 
• Represents the mountain-like abode of the gods, symbolizing spiritual ascent and divine connection.
 
• Often acts as a landmark for the community, guiding devotees to the temple.
 
 
 
• **Famous Temples with Gopurams:**
 
 
• **Meenakshi Temple (Madurai):** Known for its colorful and intricately detailed gopurams.
 
• **Brihadeeswarar Temple (Thanjavur):** Features one of the tallest gopurams in South India.
 
• **Ranganathaswamy Temple (Srirangam):** Has the tallest gopuram in India, standing at 73 meters.

questions.question: According to Census 2011, which union territory of India has the lowest population?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Lakshadweep**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• According to the Census 2011, **Lakshadweep** is the least populated Union Territory of India with a total population of **64,473**.
 
• Lakshadweep comprises **36 islands**, out of which only 10 are inhabited.
 
• The population density of Lakshadweep is **2,013 persons per square kilometer**, which is relatively high due to its small land area of just 32 square kilometers.
 
• The literacy rate in Lakshadweep is **91.85%**, which is higher than the national average.
 
• Despite its small population, Lakshadweep boasts a unique culture influenced by Islam and traditional South Indian practices.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Union Territories in India**

 
 
• India has a total of **8 Union Territories** as of 2023, including Delhi, Puducherry, and Jammu & Kashmir.
 
• Union Territories are directly governed by the **Central Government** of India.
 
• Unlike states, Union Territories have limited legislative powers, with some exceptions like Delhi and Puducherry, which have partial statehood.
 
 
 
• **Census 2011 Overview**
 
 
• The Census 2011 is the **15th National Census** of India and provides critical demographic, social, and economic data.
 
• India's total population as per Census 2011 is **1.21 billion**.
 
• The sex ratio of India stood at **940 females per 1,000 males**.
 
• The literacy rate of India was recorded as **74.04%**.
 
 
 
• **Major Islands of Lakshadweep**
 
 
• Some of the inhabited islands include **Agatti, Minicoy, Kavaratti, and Kalpeni**.
 
• Kavaratti is the **capital** of Lakshadweep.
 
• These islands are known for their **coral atolls, lagoons, and marine biodiversity**.
 
 
 
• **Tourism in Lakshadweep**
 
 
• Lakshadweep is a popular destination for **water sports** such as scuba diving, snorkeling, and kayaking.
 
• It is known for its pristine beaches and **eco-tourism** initiatives.
 
• Tourist entry to Lakshadweep is regulated, and a **special permit** is required to visit the islands.

questions.question: Which is the lengthiest written Constitution in the world?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Indian Constitution**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **Indian Constitution** is the lengthiest written Constitution in the world, with 395 articles, 12 schedules, and 22 parts at the time of its adoption in 1950.
 
• It underwent several amendments, and as of 2023, it includes **470 articles, 12 schedules, and 25 parts**, covering an extensive range of topics.
 
• The drafting of the Indian Constitution was led by the **Constituent Assembly**, chaired by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, and it took nearly **2 years, 11 months, and 18 days** to complete.
 
• The Indian Constitution draws inspiration from various global constitutions but has been uniquely tailored to the socio-economic and political needs of India.
 
• It establishes India as a **sovereign, socialist, secular, and democratic republic**, emphasizing justice, liberty, equality, and fraternity for its citizens.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Constituent Assembly:**

 
 
• The Constituent Assembly of India was established in 1946 to draft the Indian Constitution.
 
• It included representatives from various provinces and princely states, ensuring diverse participation.
 
• The assembly had 299 members at the time of adoption.
 
 
 
• **Borrowed Features:**
 
 
• The Indian Constitution adopted ideas from the constitutions of countries like the USA (fundamental rights), UK (parliamentary system), Ireland (directive principles of state policy), and Canada (federal structure).
 
 
 
• **Amendments:**
 
 
• The Indian Constitution is a living document and has been amended **105 times** as of 2023 to address changing needs.
 
• The first amendment was enacted in 1951, addressing land reforms and other socio-economic issues.
 
 
 
• **Length and Complexity:**
 
 
• The Indian Constitution is detailed and comprehensive to address India's diversity and complexities in culture, language, and governance.
 
• It includes provisions for fundamental rights, directive principles, union-state relations, emergency powers, and more.
 
 
 
• **Global Context:**
 
 
• In contrast, the US Constitution is among the shortest written constitutions with only 7 articles and 27 amendments.
 
• The British Constitution is unwritten and consists of statutes, conventions, and legal documents.

questions.question: Who wrote the novel ‘Vanity Fair’?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**William Thackeray**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **William Makepeace Thackeray** is the author of the novel **'Vanity Fair'**, which was first published in 1848.
 
• The novel is a satirical representation of British society during the early 19th century, often described as a "novel without a hero."
 
• 'Vanity Fair' primarily revolves around two main characters, Becky Sharp and Amelia Sedley, exploring themes such as ambition, morality, and social climbing.
 
• The title 'Vanity Fair' refers to an allegorical location from John Bunyan's 'Pilgrim's Progress,' symbolizing human frailty and worldly temptations.
 
• Thackeray's work is regarded as a masterpiece of English literature, showcasing his sharp wit, narrative innovation, and social critique.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **William Makepeace Thackeray**

 
 
• Thackeray (1811–1863) was a renowned English novelist and satirist, best known for his critical portrayal of English upper-class society.
 
• His other notable works include 'The History of Pendennis' and 'The Luck of Barry Lyndon.'
 
• Thackeray's literary style often involved humor, irony, and vivid character development.
 
• He was a contemporary of Charles Dickens, although their writing styles differed significantly.
 
 
 
• **Victorian Literature**
 
 
• The Victorian era (1837–1901) witnessed significant literary achievements, with authors like Charles Dickens, George Eliot, and Thackeray shaping English literature.
 
• Key themes included social reform, industrialization, class dynamics, and moral dilemmas.
 
 
 
• **Satire in Literature**
 
 
• Satire is a literary genre that uses humor, irony, and ridicule to criticize societal norms and human behavior.
 
• Thackeray's 'Vanity Fair' is considered a prime example of satire in English literature.

questions.question: Who among the following social reformers founded the Ramakrishna Mission?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Swami Vivekananda**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Swami Vivekananda** founded the Ramakrishna Mission in 1897 to propagate the teachings of his spiritual guru, **Ramakrishna Paramahamsa**.
 
• The Ramakrishna Mission focuses on **philanthropic, educational, cultural, and spiritual activities** inspired by the ideals of Vedanta.
 
• The organization is based on the principle of **"Atmano Mokshartham Jagat Hitaya Cha"**, meaning "For one's own salvation and for the welfare of the world."
 
• Its headquarters, known as **Belur Math**, is located in **Howrah, West Bengal**, on the banks of the Hooghly River.
 
• The mission operates schools, colleges, hospitals, and rural development programs in India and abroad, reflecting Swami Vivekananda's vision of social service and spiritual growth.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Ramakrishna Paramahamsa**

 
 
• He was a 19th-century Indian mystic and spiritual leader who practiced various forms of Hinduism, highlighting the unity of all religions.
 
• He emphasized the importance of direct spiritual experience over ritualistic practices.
 
• His teachings were a key inspiration for Swami Vivekananda and the founding of the Ramakrishna Mission.
 
 
 
• **Belur Math**
 
 
• It serves as the headquarters of the Ramakrishna Mission and the Ramakrishna Math.
 
• The architecture of Belur Math reflects a blend of Hindu, Islamic, Christian, and Buddhist styles, symbolizing the unity of religions.
 
 
 
• **Vedanta Philosophy**
 
 
• It is one of the six orthodox schools of Hindu philosophy, emphasizing the idea of the oneness of existence, self-realization, and the ultimate unity of all beings.
 
• The Ramakrishna Mission actively promotes Vedanta as a practical philosophy for life.
 
 
 
• **Contributions of Swami Vivekananda**
 
 
• He represented India at the **World Parliament of Religions** in Chicago in 1893, delivering a historic speech on religious tolerance and universal brotherhood.
 
• He emphasized the importance of education, social reform, and spiritual awakening for national progress.
 
• He is regarded as a key figure in the revival of Hinduism and Indian cultural identity.

questions.question: Who founded the Satya Shodhak Samaj ?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Jyotirao Phule**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Jyotirao Phule founded the **Satya Shodhak Samaj** in 1873 in Pune, Maharashtra.
 
• The primary aim of the organization was to achieve **social equality** and eradicate caste discrimination and untouchability.
 
• Satya Shodhak Samaj focused on spreading education and promoting rational thinking, especially among **lower-caste communities.**
 
• Phule was a pioneer of social reform and worked to uplift marginalized sections, including women and Dalits, through his initiatives.
 
• The organization emphasized the values of justice, equality, and universal human rights, rejecting religious orthodoxy and caste hierarchies.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Jyotirao Phule**

 
 
• He is widely regarded as one of the first prominent social reformers in India who fought against casteism and patriarchy.
 
• Phule and his wife, Savitribai Phule, are known for their contributions to women’s education and empowerment in India.
 
• He authored several works, including the seminal book **"Gulamgiri"** (Slavery), which criticized caste oppression.
 
• Jyotirao Phule was also the first person to use the term **"Dalit"** to describe marginalized communities.
 
 
 
• **Satya Shodhak Samaj's Objectives**
 
 
• The organization aimed to create a society based on principles of **equality, liberty, and fraternity.**
 
• It rejected Brahmanical dominance, advocating for self-respect and dignity for all castes.
 
• It encouraged members to perform marriages without priests and rituals, emphasizing rationalism and simplicity.
 
 
 
• **Impact of Satya Shodhak Samaj**

questions.question: The Directive Principles of State Policy resembles the ‘Instrument of Instructions’ enumerated in the ___________.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP) in the Indian Constitution were influenced by the **'Instrument of Instructions' mentioned in the Government of India Act, 1935**.
 
• The 'Instrument of Instructions' served as guidelines for the Governor-General and Governors in matters of governance under the Government of India Act, 1935.
 
• Similarly, the DPSPs act as **guiding principles for the state** in India to ensure socio-economic justice, equity, and welfare policies.
 
• The DPSPs are enumerated in **Part IV of the Indian Constitution** and are not enforceable by the courts but fundamental to governance.
 
• The Government of India Act, 1935, is considered a significant precursor to the Constitution of India, providing a blueprint for several constitutional provisions.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP):**

 
 
• DPSPs are guidelines for the state to formulate policies aimed at achieving socio-economic justice and welfare.
 
• They are inspired by the Irish Constitution, which borrowed concepts from the Spanish Constitution.
 
• DPSPs include principles related to social justice, economic welfare, foreign policy, and legal and administrative matters.
 
• They are non-justiciable, meaning they cannot be enforced by a court of law.
 
 
 
• **Government of India Act, 1935:**
 
 
• This act introduced provincial autonomy, a federal structure, and an Instrument of Instructions for the British-administered provinces.
 
• It was the most comprehensive constitutional reform before Indian independence.
 
• Many provisions of the Indian Constitution, such as federalism and the division of powers, are derived from this act.
 
 
 
• **Instrument of Instructions:**
 
 
• The Instrument of Instructions was a set of guidelines for the Governor-General and Governors under the Government of India Act, 1935.
 
• It outlined the principles to be followed in governance, similar to the DPSPs in the Indian Constitution.
 
 
 
• **Relation Between DPSPs and Fundamental Rights:**
 
 
• While Fundamental Rights are justiciable and enforceable by the courts, DPSPs are non-justiciable.
 
• Both aim to establish a framework for a welfare state, ensuring justice, liberty, and equality for all citizens.

questions.question: From which of the following countries did India adopt the ‘procedure established by the law’?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Japan**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The term **"procedure established by law"** is derived from the Japanese Constitution, which India adopted during the drafting of its Constitution.
 
• The phrase is enshrined in Article 21 of the Indian Constitution, guaranteeing the protection of life and personal liberty.
 
• Unlike the "due process of law" adopted by the US, "procedure established by law" emphasizes adherence to the process defined by the legislature, irrespective of its fairness or reasonableness.
 
• The framers of the Indian Constitution deliberately chose this concept to avoid judicial overreach, ensuring legislative supremacy during the initial years post-independence.
 
• This concept highlights the importance of legislative procedures in ensuring legal compliance, even if it doesn't directly address the principles of justice or equity.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Procedure Established by Law:**

 
 
• It means that a law duly enacted by the legislature or governing body is valid if it follows the correct procedure, even if it is unjust or unfair.
 
• The judiciary ensures compliance with the procedure but does not evaluate the law's moral or ethical aspects.
 
 
 
• **Due Process of Law:**
 
 
• Unlike "procedure established by law," this concept (used in the US Constitution) allows courts to assess both the procedural and substantive aspects of a law.
 
• It provides greater protection of individual rights by ensuring fairness, justice, and reasonableness in laws.
 
 
 
• **Article 21 of the Indian Constitution:**
 
 
• States that "No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law."
 
• This article has been interpreted expansively by the Supreme Court of India to include rights such as privacy, clean environment, and dignity.
 
 
 
• **Judicial Evolution in India:**
 
 
• Over time, the Indian judiciary has interpreted "procedure established by law" to incorporate elements of fairness, reasonableness, and justice, bringing it closer to "due process of law."
 
• The landmark case **Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978)** marked a significant shift in this interpretation.

• The Chief Minister of Delhi is appointed by the **President of India** under Article 239AA of the Indian Constitution.
 
• The appointment is made following the recommendation of the party or coalition with the majority in the Delhi Legislative Assembly.
 
• Though the President formally appoints the Chief Minister, the **Lieutenant Governor of Delhi** administers the oath of office.
 
• The Chief Minister is the head of the Council of Ministers in Delhi and holds executive powers within the jurisdiction of the Delhi NCT (National Capital Territory).

• **Lieutenant Governor of Delhi:**

• **Kushana Empire:**

• **Religious Patronage:**

• **Art and Architecture:**

questions.question: In a food chain, the base of energy pyramid consists of:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**producers**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• In a food chain, **producers form the base** of the energy pyramid, as they are the primary source of energy for all other trophic levels.
 
• Producers are typically **autotrophic organisms**, such as plants, algae, and certain bacteria, that can synthesize their own food through photosynthesis or chemosynthesis.
 
• They convert solar energy into chemical energy stored in organic compounds, forming the foundation of the ecosystem's energy flow.
 
• The energy transfer between trophic levels is highly inefficient, with only about **10% of energy** being passed on to the next level, making producers critical for sustaining the ecosystem.
 
• Examples of producers include grass in a grassland ecosystem, phytoplankton in aquatic ecosystems, and trees in a forest ecosystem.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Energy Pyramid:**

 
 
• An energy pyramid is a graphical representation of the energy flow within an ecosystem.
 
• It is divided into trophic levels, starting with producers at the base, followed by primary consumers, secondary consumers, and tertiary consumers.
 
• The width of each level represents the amount of energy available at that trophic level.
 
 
 
• **Trophic Levels:**
 
 
• Trophic levels refer to the hierarchical stages in a food chain, starting with producers (first level) and moving up to herbivores, carnivores, and apex predators.
 
• Energy transfer between these levels follows the 10% rule, where only 10% of energy from one level is passed to the next.
 
 
 
• **Photosynthesis:**
 
 
• Photosynthesis is the process by which producers convert solar energy, water, and carbon dioxide into glucose and oxygen.
 
• This chemical energy stored in glucose provides the foundation for the entire food chain.
 
 
 
• **Consumers:**
 
 
• Consumers depend on producers or other organisms for energy. They include primary consumers (herbivores), secondary consumers (carnivores), and tertiary consumers (top predators).
 
• Unlike producers, consumers cannot synthesize their own food and rely on external sources of energy.
 
 
 
• **Decomposers:**
 
 
• Decomposers, such as fungi and bacteria, break down organic matter from dead organisms, recycling nutrients back into the ecosystem.
 
• They play a critical role in maintaining the balance of the ecosystem by facilitating nutrient cycling.

questions.question: Who among the following social reformers developed the modern Bengali Alphabet in British India?

__
 
• **Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar** was a prominent social reformer, educationist, and writer of the 19th century in British India.
 
• He played a key role in the development of the **modern Bengali alphabet** and its rationalization, making it simpler and more accessible.
 
• Vidyasagar introduced **typographical standardization** of Bengali script, which included the introduction of punctuation and elimination of redundant characters.
 
• His work on Bengali grammar and script greatly influenced the **modernization of the Bengali language** and its usage in literature and education.
 
• He is also remembered for his contributions to **women’s education and widow remarriage** in India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Bengali Alphabet**

 
 
• The Bengali script is derived from the ancient **Brahmi script**, and its development was influenced by the Nagari and Siddham scripts.
 
• The modern Bengali alphabet consists of **11 vowels** and **39 consonants**.
 
• Vidyasagar’s contributions helped standardize the script, making it suitable for printing and education.
 
 
 
• **Social Reforms by Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar**
 
 
• He was a staunch advocate for the **widow remarriage movement** in India, leading to the passage of the Widow Remarriage Act of 1856.

• **His Contributions to Literature and Education**

• He was instrumental in **modernizing the education system** in Bengal by introducing Western methodologies and rational thinking.
 
 
 
• **Legacy**
 
 
• Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar is fondly remembered as the **“Father of Bengali Prose”** for his contributions to the language.
 
• He is also regarded as one of the key architects of the Bengal Renaissance, which marked a period of cultural and intellectual awakening in 19th-century India.

• The focus on reducing the gender gap in literacy was part of a broader strategy for achieving inclusive growth and social equity during the plan period.
 
• Programs like **Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan (SSA)** and **National Literacy Mission (NLM)** were strengthened to address the disparity in literacy rates between men and women.

questions.question: In which year was the National Rural Health Mission launched in India to provide accessible, affordable and quality health care to the rural population?

__
 
• The National Rural Health Mission (NRHM) was launched by the Government of India in **April 2005**.
 
• It aimed to provide accessible, affordable, and quality healthcare services to the rural population, especially vulnerable groups.
 
• NRHM focused on improving maternal and child health, reducing mortality rates, and combating communicable and non-communicable diseases.
 
• The mission emphasized strengthening the public health system, including infrastructure, human resources, and service delivery in rural areas.
 
• NRHM was later subsumed under the **National Health Mission (NHM)** in 2013, which expanded its scope to urban areas as well.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Key Objectives of NRHM:**

 
 
• Reduce infant mortality rate (IMR) and maternal mortality rate (MMR).
 
• Ensure universal access to public health services such as immunization, nutrition, sanitation, and safe drinking water.
 
• Promote population stabilization and address gender and social disparities in healthcare.
 
 
 
• **Accredited Social Health Activists (ASHAs):**
 
 
• NRHM introduced ASHAs, community health workers, to act as a link between rural communities and healthcare systems.
 
• ASHAs are trained to provide basic healthcare services and facilitate awareness on health and hygiene.
 
 
 
• **Infrastructure Development:**
 
 
• Under NRHM, efforts were made to upgrade rural healthcare facilities such as Sub-Centres, Primary Health Centres (PHCs), and Community Health Centres (CHCs).
 
• Mobile Medical Units (MMUs) were also introduced to provide healthcare services in remote areas.
 
 
 
• **National Health Mission (NHM):**
 
 
• NHM, launched in 2013, combined NRHM with the National Urban Health Mission (NUHM).
 
• NHM expanded its focus to urban health challenges while continuing NRHM's objectives in rural areas.

questions.question: The Nizam Shahi dynasty of Ahmednagar was founded by ________ in 1490.

questions.question: Which Article of the Constitution of India is associated with the protection and improvement of the environment and safeguarding of forests and wild life?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 48 A**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Article 48 A** of the Constitution of India is part of the Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP) under Part IV.
 
• It mandates the State to **protect and improve the environment** and to safeguard the forests and wildlife of the country.
 
• This Article was added through the **42nd Amendment Act, 1976**, which is considered a landmark amendment in Indian constitutional history.
 
• It reflects the commitment of the Indian Constitution towards **environmental conservation and sustainable development**.
 
• Article 48 A lays the foundation for various environmental protection laws and policies implemented in India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976**

 
 
• Known as the "Mini-Constitution," this amendment introduced significant changes, including the addition of Article 48 A and Article 51 A (Fundamental Duties).
 
• It emphasized environmental protection as a key responsibility of both the State and citizens.
 
 
 
• **Article 51 A (g)**
 
 
• It is a Fundamental Duty that requires every citizen of India to **protect and improve the natural environment, including forests, lakes, rivers, and wildlife**.
 
• Citizens are also obligated to have compassion for living creatures.
 
 
 
• **Environmental Legislation in India**
 
 
• Key laws include the **Environment Protection Act, 1986**, **Wildlife Protection Act, 1972**, and the **Forest Conservation Act, 1980**.
 
• These laws derive their constitutional backing from Articles 48 A and 51 A (g).
 
 
 
• **Global Environmental Commitments**
 
 
• India is a signatory to major international agreements such as the **Paris Agreement** under the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC).
 
• The principles enshrined in Article 48 A align with global goals for sustainable development and climate action.

questions.question: In the northern hemisphere, summer solstice occurs on:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**21st June**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **summer solstice** in the northern hemisphere occurs on **21st June** each year.
 
• It marks the **longest day and shortest night** of the year in the northern hemisphere.
 
• This event happens when the Earth's axial tilt is closest to the Sun, and the Sun appears at its highest point in the sky at noon.
 
• The summer solstice is also referred to as the **"June solstice"** in the northern hemisphere.
 
• It is an astronomical event that signals the beginning of summer in many cultures and is celebrated in various traditions worldwide.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Solstice**: The term "solstice" is derived from the Latin words "sol" (sun) and "sistere" (to stand still), referring to the Sun's apparent pause in movement along the horizon.
 
• **Earth's axial tilt**: The Earth's axis is tilted at an angle of approximately 23.5 degrees, which causes the variation in sunlight received by different parts of the Earth throughout the year.
 
• **Equinox vs. Solstice**: While solstices mark the longest or shortest days of the year, equinoxes occur when day and night are approximately equal in length.
 
• **Winter Solstice**: In contrast to the summer solstice, the winter solstice occurs around 21st December in the northern hemisphere and marks the shortest day and longest night of the year.
 
• **Cultural significance**: The summer solstice has been celebrated in various cultures through festivals and rituals, such as Midsummer in Scandinavian countries and Inti Raymi in the Andes.

__
 
• The Losar Festival is celebrated in **Ladakh**, a Union Territory in India, marking the Tibetan New Year.
 
• It is observed by the **Buddhist community** and marks the beginning of the lunisolar Tibetan calendar.
 
• The festival typically falls in **December or January** (based on the Tibetan calendar) and lasts for 15 days, with major celebrations during the first three days.
 
• Losar is characterized by **prayers, traditional music, dance performances, and unique rituals** to ward off evil spirits and bring prosperity.
 
• It is celebrated with great enthusiasm, including the preparation of traditional dishes like **guthuk** (a noodle soup) and the offering of **tsampa** (barley flour) to deities.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Losar's Historical Significance:**

 
 
• The festival has its roots in the pre-Buddhist Bon religion of Tibet, where rituals were performed to drive away evil spirits at the end of the year.
 
• After the advent of Buddhism, these traditions were incorporated into the Buddhist New Year celebrations.
 
 
 
• **Major Rituals and Practices:**
 
 
• Cleaning homes and monasteries to symbolize removing negativity and inviting good fortune.
 
• Lighting butter lamps and performing **Cham dances**, which are sacred masked dances by monks.
 
• Offering prayers to deities like **Palden Lhamo**, the protector goddess.
 
 
 
• **Buddhist Influence:**
 
 
• Losar is deeply tied to Tibetan Buddhism and reflects its cultural and spiritual ethos.
 
• The festival emphasizes **compassion, harmony, and gratitude** towards nature and the divine.
 
 
 
• **Geographic Importance:**
 
 
• Besides Ladakh, Losar is also celebrated in other Himalayan regions, including **Arunachal Pradesh, Sikkim, and parts of Himachal Pradesh**.
 
• It showcases the rich cultural diversity of India and its deep connection to Buddhist traditions.

questions.question: Faiyyaz Khan, Latafat Hussein Khan and Dinkar Kaikini are famous exponents from which of the following Gharanas?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Agra Gharana**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Faiyyaz Khan, Latafat Hussein Khan, and Dinkar Kaikini are celebrated exponents of the **Agra Gharana**, a prominent school of Hindustani classical music.
 
• The **Agra Gharana** is known for its unique blend of dhrupad and khayal styles, emphasizing intricate layakari (rhythmic interplay) and bol-baant (syllabic patterns).
 
• Faiyyaz Khan, a legendary vocalist of the Agra Gharana, was one of the most influential figures in the history of Hindustani classical music.
 
• Agra Gharana traces its origins back to the 14th century, with its roots in the dhrupad tradition and contributions from musicians like Nayak Gopal and Nayak Khanderao.
 
• The Gharana emphasizes a powerful voice culture and extensive use of meend (gliding notes) in its renditions.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Gharanas in Hindustani Classical Music:**

 
 
• Gharanas are schools or styles of Hindustani classical music, each having distinct characteristics and traditions.
 
• Prominent Gharanas include Agra, Jaipur-Atrauli, Kirana, Benaras, and Patiala, among others.
 
• Each Gharana specializes in unique techniques, such as voice modulation, improvisation, and rhythmic patterns.
 
 
 
• **Dhrupad and Khayal:**
 
 
• Dhrupad is the oldest vocal style in Hindustani classical music, characterized by its solemn and meditative nature.
 
• Khayal, meaning "imagination," is a more flexible and expressive style that evolved from dhrupad.
 
• The Agra Gharana blends both styles, retaining the depth of dhrupad while exploring the creativity of khayal.
 
 
 
• **Faiyyaz Khan:**
 
 
• Faiyyaz Khan was awarded the title "Aftab-e-Mousiqui" (Sun of Music) for his unparalleled contribution to Hindustani classical music.
 
• His renditions were marked by powerful voice projection and intricate rhythmic elaborations.
 
 
 
• **Other Exponents:**

questions.question: WTO was formed in the year 1995 to replace which of the following institutions?

options.text: Industrial Board of Reconstruction and Development
General Agreement of Trade and Tariff

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**General Agreement of Trade and Tariff**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The World Trade Organization (WTO) was established on **1 January 1995**, replacing the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT).
 
• GATT was created in **1948** as a legal agreement between multiple nations to promote international trade by reducing or eliminating trade barriers such as tariffs or quotas.
 
• WTO expanded the scope of GATT by incorporating agreements on services (GATS) and intellectual property (TRIPS).
 
• The WTO serves as a forum for trade negotiations, dispute resolution, and enforcement of trade agreements among member countries.
 
• As of 2023, the WTO has **164 member countries**, accounting for over 98% of global trade.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Functions of WTO:**

 
 
• Administers trade agreements and ensures their implementation by member countries.
 
• Provides a platform for trade negotiations to enhance global trade liberalization.
 
• Resolves trade disputes between member nations through its dispute settlement mechanism.
 
• Monitors global trade policies and provides technical assistance to developing countries.
 
 
 
• **GATT Overview:**
 
 
• GATT was a multilateral agreement aimed at promoting international trade by reducing tariffs and other trade barriers.
 
• It underwent eight rounds of negotiations, with the last being the Uruguay Round (1986–1994), which led to the creation of the WTO.
 
• GATT primarily dealt with trade in goods, whereas the WTO expanded its scope to include services and intellectual property.
 
 
 
• **Key Agreements under WTO:**
 
 
• **GATS:** General Agreement on Trade in Services focuses on trade in services.
 
• **TRIPS:** Agreement on Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights sets minimum standards for intellectual property regulation.
 
• **Agreement on Agriculture (AoA):** Addresses agricultural trade policies including subsidies, market access, and export competition.
 
 
 
• **Criticism of WTO:**
 
 
• Accused of favoring developed countries at the expense of developing nations.
 
• Critics argue that its policies promote corporate interests over environmental and labor rights.
 
• Decision-making is often criticized for being non-inclusive, with smaller economies having limited influence.

questions.question: What process was discovered in the early 1990s that is currently used to remove ammonia from wastewater and contributes significantly to the loss of fixed nitrogen from the oceans?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Anammox**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__

• **Anammox (Anaerobic Ammonium Oxidation)** is a biological process that was discovered in the early 1990s.

• This process is used to remove ammonia from wastewater by converting it into nitrogen gas under anaerobic conditions.

• Anammox bacteria are capable of oxidizing ammonium using nitrite as an electron acceptor, producing nitrogen gas.

• Anammox contributes significantly to the loss of fixed nitrogen in marine ecosystems, especially in oxygen-depleted zones.

• It is a cost-effective and environmentally friendly alternative to traditional nitrogen removal methods.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• **Nitrogen Cycle:**

• The nitrogen cycle is a biogeochemical process that transforms nitrogen into various chemical forms, including ammonium, nitrite, nitrate, and nitrogen gas.

• Anammox plays a key role in the nitrogen cycle by converting fixed nitrogen compounds back into atmospheric nitrogen.

• **Anammox Bacteria:**

• Anammox bacteria belong to the Planctomycetes phylum and thrive in anaerobic environments such as wastewater treatment plants and marine sediments.

• Their unique cell structure contains a special organelle known as the "anammoxosome," where the process occurs.

• **Environmental Impact:**

• Anammox reduces the need for chemical additives in wastewater treatment, lowering operational costs and environmental pollution.

• It helps mitigate eutrophication in aquatic ecosystems by reducing nitrogen runoff into water bodies.

• **Applications in Industry:**

• Anammox technology is widely used in modern wastewater treatment systems for nitrogen removal.

• Its adoption has grown due to its high efficiency and sustainability compared to conventional processes like nitrification-denitrification.

questions.question: Which of the following Harappan structures had a thin lining of bitumen to prevent the seepage of water ?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Great Bath**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Great Bath is one of the most prominent architectural structures found in the Harappan civilization, located in Mohenjo-Daro (present-day Pakistan).
 
• The structure was designed as a large water tank made of baked bricks and featured a thin lining of bitumen to make it waterproof and prevent water seepage.
 
• The Great Bath is believed to have been used for ritualistic or religious purposes, as water held a significant cultural and spiritual value in ancient Harappan society.
 
• It measures approximately 12 meters in length, 7 meters in width, and 2.4 meters in depth, with steps leading into the tank on both ends.
 
• This structure highlights the advanced engineering and urban planning skills of the Harappan people, especially in water management and drainage systems.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Bitumen in Harappan Structures:**

 
 
• Bitumen, also known as natural asphalt, was used as a waterproofing agent in Harappan architecture.
 
• It was applied as a thin layer to prevent water from seeping into the walls or floors of structures like the Great Bath.
 
 
 
• **Urban Planning of Harappa:**
 
 
• The Harappans were known for their well-planned cities, which included wide roads, drainage systems, and standardized brick sizes.
 
• Public structures like granaries, baths, and assembly halls were an integral part of their urban design.
 
 
 
• **Ritual Significance of Water:**
 
 
• Water played an essential role in the religious and cultural practices of the Harappan civilization.
 
• The Great Bath may have been a site for communal or ceremonial purification rituals involving water.
 
 
 
• **Other Notable Harappan Structures:**
 
 
• Granaries were used for storing surplus grains and were located near agricultural areas or riverbanks.
 
• The drainage systems were highly advanced, with covered channels to carry away wastewater from residential areas.
 
 
 
• **Discovery and Excavation:**
 
 
• Mohenjo-Daro was discovered in 1922 by archaeologist R. D. Banerji.
 
• The excavation revealed significant insights into the social, economic, and cultural aspects of the Harappan civilization.

questions.question: Under competitive assets market condition, the price of a bond must always be ______________ to its present value in equilibrium.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**equal**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Under competitive market conditions, the price of a bond in equilibrium is always **equal to its present value**, which is calculated based on discounted future cash flows.
 
• The present value is determined using the **market interest rate**, also referred to as the discount rate.
 
• The equilibrium condition ensures that the bond price reflects its intrinsic value, preventing **arbitrage opportunities**.
 
• If the bond price deviates from its present value, market forces will adjust the price to restore equilibrium.
 
• This principle is rooted in the concept of **efficient markets**, where asset prices fully reflect all available information.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Bond Pricing:**

 
 
• Bonds are priced based on their future cash flows, including periodic coupon payments and the principal repayment at maturity.
 
• The present value of these cash flows is calculated using the prevailing **market interest rate**.
 
• A higher market interest rate results in a lower present value (and price), while a lower interest rate increases the present value.
 
 
 
• **Efficient Market Hypothesis (EMH):**
 
 
• This theory states that asset prices reflect all available information, ensuring no persistent arbitrage opportunities.
 
• Bond prices under competitive market conditions align with their intrinsic value, supporting EMH.
 
 
 
• **Discount Rate:**
 
 
• The discount rate is the interest rate used to calculate the present value of future cash flows.
 
• It reflects the opportunity cost of capital and market risk.
 
 
 
• **Arbitrage:**
 
 
• Arbitrage refers to the practice of profiting from price discrepancies in different markets.
 
• In competitive markets, bond prices adjust quickly to eliminate arbitrage opportunities.

questions.question: Which letter code of Köppen climate characterises a hot-summer humid continental climate?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Dfa**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Dfa** is the Köppen climate classification code for a hot-summer humid continental climate.
 
• Regions with a **Dfa climate** experience hot, humid summers and cold, snowy winters.
 
• These climates are typically found in the interior regions of continents, away from oceanic influences.
 
• Examples of areas with Dfa climates include parts of the Midwestern United States, southeastern Canada, and northern China.
 
• The classification is defined by average temperatures above **22°C** (72°F) in the warmest month and below **-3°C** (27°F) in the coldest month.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Köppen Climate Classification**

 
 
• A widely used climate classification system developed by climatologist Wladimir Köppen in 1884.
 
• It categorizes climates based on average monthly and annual temperature and precipitation.
 
• The system includes five main climate groups: Tropical (A), Dry (B), Temperate (C), Continental (D), and Polar (E).
 
• Subcategories further refine the classification based on seasonal patterns and temperature variations.
 
 
 
• **Continental Climates (Group D)**
 
 
• Characterized by significant seasonal temperature variations due to their location far from oceanic moderating effects.
 
• These climates are divided into subtypes like Dfa (hot-summer), Dfb (warm-summer), and Dfc (cold-summer).
 
• Typically found in the interiors of continents, such as North America, Europe, and Asia.
 
 
 
• **Hot-Summer Humid Continental Climate (Dfa)**
 
 
• Defined by hot summers with average temperatures above 22°C (72°F).
 
• Winters are cold, with temperatures frequently dropping below freezing.
 
• Precipitation is evenly distributed throughout the year, with occasional snow during winter months.
 
 
 
• **Examples of Dfa Regions**
 
 
• Midwestern United States (e.g., Chicago, Detroit).
 
• Southeastern Canada (e.g., Toronto, Ottawa).
 
• Northern China (e.g., Beijing).
 
• Parts of Eastern Europe (e.g., Kyiv).

questions.question: According to the seventh schedule of the Indian Constitution, Agriculture is in which list?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**State List**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Seventh Schedule of the Indian Constitution divides the powers and functions of the government into three lists: **Union List, State List, and Concurrent List**.
 
• Agriculture is exclusively mentioned under the **State List in Entry 14**.
 
• The State List empowers state governments to make laws and policies regarding agricultural matters, as it is considered a state subject.
 
• Subjects under the State List include land improvement, agricultural education, research, protection of plants, and other agricultural matters.
 
• The Union government has limited interference in agricultural matters unless they overlap with subjects in the Concurrent List or in cases of national importance.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Union List:**

 
 
• This list contains subjects of national importance such as defense, foreign affairs, atomic energy, and banking.
 
• Only the Parliament of India can make laws on subjects in the Union List.
 
 
 
• **State List:**
 
 
• This list contains subjects of local or state importance such as police, public health, and agriculture.
 
• State legislatures have exclusive power to legislate on these subjects.
 
 
 
• **Concurrent List:**
 
 
• This list includes subjects where both the Union and State governments can legislate, such as education, forests, and marriage.
 
• In case of conflict, the Union law prevails over the state law.
 
 
 
• **Important Agricultural Initiatives:**
 
 
• Although agriculture is a state subject, national-level schemes like PM-KISAN and Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (PMFBY) are implemented by the Union government.
 
• These schemes aim to provide financial support and insurance to farmers across India.
 
 
 
• **Significance of Agriculture:**
 
 
• Agriculture is a crucial sector in India, employing over 50% of the workforce and contributing around 18% to the GDP.
 
• The decentralization of agricultural policymaking allows states to address region-specific issues effectively.

questions.question: Who among the following does NOT participate in the election of the President of India?

options.text: Elected members of legislative council of state

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Elected members of legislative council of state**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The President of India is elected by an electoral college consisting of **the elected members** of both Houses of Parliament and the elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of States and Union territories (with legislatures).
 
• The **legislative councils** in states, where they exist, are not involved in the process as their members are not part of the electoral college.
 
• Legislative councils are the **upper houses** in bicameral legislatures of some Indian states and have limited roles in legislative and governance processes.
 
• This arrangement ensures a wider representation of the country’s federal structure while excluding unelected members from participating in the Presidential election.
 
• Hence, **elected members of the legislative council** do not participate in the election of the President of India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Electoral College for Presidential Election:**

 
 
• The electoral college comprises **only elected representatives** from the Lok Sabha, Rajya Sabha, and State/Union Territory Legislative Assemblies.
 
• Nominated members of Parliament and state legislatures are excluded, as are members of legislative councils.
 
 
 
• **States with Legislative Councils:**
 
 
• As of now, only six states in India have legislative councils: **Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra, Bihar, and Karnataka.**
 
• These councils serve as advisory bodies, with members elected through indirect elections or nominated by the Governor.
 
 
 
• **Presidential Election Process:**
 
 
• The election follows the **proportional representation system** through a single transferable vote.
 
• Each vote carries a value based on the population of the state or Union Territory the voter represents.
 
 
 
• **Role of Legislative Councils:**
 
 
• Legislative councils primarily act as a **review body** for legislation passed by the legislative assemblies.
 
• They have no direct role in the election of the President of India.

questions.question: In which Budget was Disinvestment Fund and Asset Management Company set up?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Tue Apr 01 2003 00:00:00 GMT+0530 (India Standard Time)**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Disinvestment Fund and Asset Management Company were set up in the **Union Budget of 2003-04**.
 
• The primary goal of establishing the Disinvestment Fund was to channelize proceeds from the disinvestment of public sector enterprises (PSEs) for productive use.
 
• The Asset Management Company was introduced to professionally manage assets of public sector undertakings (PSUs) that were being disinvested.
 
• This step was in alignment with the Indian government's broader agenda of economic reforms and reducing the fiscal deficit.
 
• The initiative was overseen by the Ministry of Disinvestment, which was later merged with the Ministry of Finance in 2004.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Disinvestment:**

 
 
• Disinvestment refers to the sale or liquidation of government-owned assets, typically public sector enterprises (PSEs).
 
• The objective is to reduce fiscal burden, improve operational efficiency, and encourage private sector participation.
 
• It also helps in raising funds for the government, which can be utilized for developmental or budgetary needs.
 
 
 
• **Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs):**
 
 
• PSUs are government-owned corporations where the majority stake (51% or more) is held by the central or state government.
 
• They are established to ensure that essential goods and services are available to citizens at affordable costs.
 
• Examples include Bharat Heavy Electricals Limited (BHEL) and Steel Authority of India Limited (SAIL).
 
 
 
• **Fiscal Deficit:**
 
 
• It occurs when the government's total expenditure exceeds its total revenue, excluding borrowings.
 
• Reducing the fiscal deficit is essential for maintaining macroeconomic stability and ensuring sustainable growth.
 
 
 
• **Economic Reforms:**
 
 
• Economic reforms in India, initiated in 1991, include liberalization, privatization, and globalization (LPG model).
 
• Disinvestment of PSEs is a crucial aspect of these reforms, aimed at reducing government control over industries and fostering competition.

questions.question: The most common route for MNC investment is to buy up ________.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**local companies**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Multinational Corporations (MNCs) commonly invest in **local companies** as it provides a quick entry into the market.
 
• Acquiring local companies helps MNCs leverage existing **infrastructure, networks, and brand recognition** of the acquired firms.
 
• This route allows MNCs to overcome **regulatory barriers** and gain access to the local market’s customer base more efficiently.
 
• Mergers and acquisitions of local companies enable MNCs to obtain **local expertise and skilled human resources**, which are crucial for navigating regional market dynamics.
 
• Examples include Facebook’s acquisition of Indian startup Meesho and Walmart’s acquisition of Flipkart, signaling strategic investment in local companies to strengthen their foothold in emerging markets.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Multinational Corporations (MNCs)**

 
 
• MNCs are companies that operate in multiple countries but are headquartered in one specific country.
 
• They play a significant role in global trade and often influence economic policies in host countries.
 
• Examples include Apple, Amazon, Google, Unilever, and Toyota.
 
 
 
• **Benefits of Acquiring Local Companies**
 
 
• Facilitates market entry by utilizing the existing customer base and brand loyalty.
 
• Helps in adapting to **local culture and consumer preferences**.
 
• Reduces operational risks by leveraging local expertise and infrastructure.
 
 
 
• **Challenges Faced by MNCs in Local Investments**
 
 
• Regulatory and legal hurdles in host countries.
 
• Integration challenges between the MNC and the acquired company due to differences in corporate culture.
 
• Potential backlash from local communities or governments against foreign ownership.
 
 
 
• **Alternative Routes for MNC Investment**
 
 
• Establishing wholly-owned subsidiaries in the host country.
 
• Entering joint ventures with local partners to share risks and resources.
 
• Developing strategic alliances to leverage complementary strengths without ownership changes.
